text.p: BOSTON (reuter) - During recent months, many investors have poured their money into mutual funds that invest in the hottest sectors of the stock market.

The investors are drawn by stellar performance numbers at funds such as Janus Olympus, which has attracted $450 million in new assets since its inception last December, and Warburg Pincus Post-Venture Capital, which has seen $150 million in new investment in its first year.

Trouble is, shareholders who chase hot funds often get burned. For example, a fund that has been outpacing the market may owe its results to strong gains in a particular sector -- for example, health care or technology. The fund could suffer sharp losses when that sector loses steam.
A better strategy is to check out funds that have delivered mediocre results in the recent past.

The reason is that funds that recently have trailed their competitors may be investing in out-of-favour corners of the market. Such corners often hold bargains that can provide strong gains when they suddenly catch Wall Street's eye.

Naturally, you'll find some perennial losers among funds that are trailing their peers in today's market. You can avoid those habitual clunkers by choosing funds whose recent troubles are offset by superior long-term records.
A quick survey of Morningstar Mutual Funds' database turns up 113 funds that meet these two criteria:
First, they have delivered superior risk-adjusted returns over the past five years.
Second, their one-year returns through September put them in the bottom half of funds that share their investment objective.
Among growth funds, the survey turned up AIM Value A (800-347-4246; $500 minimum investment; 5.5 percent load).

The fund has delivered 17.7 percent annual returns during the past five years and been only about 75 percent as volatile as its average peer; however, it gained only 5.3 percent during the recent 12-month period vs. 16.3 percent for the typical growth fund. AIM Value's portfolio managers focus on shares of neglected or out-of-favour firms on the verge of posting stronger earnings that will draw investors' attention.
But unlike many funds that stick with such stocks once they become hot, this one sells them when the share values become inflated.

The fund's popularity worked against it during 1996. As large amounts of cash flowed into its coffers, the managers had trouble finding bargains that met their criteria. The fund's cash holdings swelled to 25 percent, which hurt its performance as stock market averages soared.

AIM Value also suffered from its stake in defensive stocks of firms in industries such as utilities and pharmaceuticals as well as some financial services. But it seems likely that such shares will perform well in the months ahead, as investors compare their valuations to those of stocks in overheated sectors of the market.
An even better-known laggard is Gabelli Asset (800-422-3554; $1,000 minimum investment; 0.25 percent load), run by respected value investor Mario Gabelli.

The fund turned in a 12.4 percent return during the 12 months through September. It has lagged other growth funds during the period, in part because it shuns stocks that are driven by earnings momentum. Instead, Gabelli likes shares of companies that seem undervalued based on factors such as cash flow or the long-term growth prospects in their industry.
Gabelli's keen eye for value has led the fund to strong gains during the past decade; moreover, it has been only about 60 percent as volatile as the typical equity fund.

Thus, while his picks may trail the average fund managers' from time to time, it seems likely that patient shareholders will be well-rewarded -- especially if they buy into the fund when many of its holdings are out of the limelight.
Finally, Neuberger & Berman Guardian (800-877-9700; $1,000 minimum investment; no-load) stands out among top growth-and-income funds that have suffered poor returns during the past year.
The fund has gained 16 percent annually during the past five years, and has been only about three-quarters as volatile as other funds in its category, according to Morningstar.

The fund's large investments in financial and technology stocks hurt performance early in 1996, but such problems are rare under seasoned managers Kent Simons and Larry Marx. More often, the managers' sector bets lead them to outsized gains. Such gains will likely continue in the long run, given the managers' proven ability to find good value among a variety of stocks, ranging from cyclicals such as Chrysler to growth entries such as Compaq Computer.
(EDITORS: Clint Willis is a freelance writer who covers financial issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Willis.)
